questions.q: You register GET /tasks/:slug and then GET /tasks/:taskId. What does the router do?
questions.explain: Only a second route with the same method and pattern is a conflict. A route that is shadowed by an equally specific earlier one is accepted silently, which is why a route-table test with router.match is worth writing.
options: Throws RouteConflictError, because both match the same paths
Accepts both; the second can never answer a request
Replaces the first route with the second
Merges them so both names are set in ctx.params

questions.explain: GET and POST on /tasks are different routes. The second GET is an exact duplicate, so it throws a RouteConflictError and is not added; two routes remain.

questions.q: Only this route is registered. What does this print?
questions.explain: A wildcard captures the whole rest of the path, slashes included, and it also matches an empty rest. So /files itself reaches the route with an empty path.

questions.q: For the route /tasks/:id and the request /tasks/042, what is ctx.params.id?
questions.explain: Route parameters are always decoded strings. Turning "042" into a number, and deciding whether leading zeros are allowed, is your code's job.

questions.explain: caf%C3%A9 decodes to café and matches. An encoded slash would smuggle a / into one parameter, so that segment never matches and the request finds no route.

questions.q: Why does the router refuse a segment such as a%2Fb instead of passing "a/b" to :id?
questions.explain: One parameter should be one path segment. Letting an encoded slash through turns :id into a multi-segment value, which is the start of many path traversal bugs.
options: Because percent-encoding is not allowed in URLs
Because parameters may not contain letters and slashes together
A handler that puts the value into a file path or another URL could be led somewhere the route was never meant to reach

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: buildRoutePath encodes every value, so a space becomes %20 and a slash %2F. The value stays one segment and cannot change the shape of the path.

questions.q: You registered only GET /tasks/:id. A client sends HEAD /tasks/1. What happens by default?
questions.explain: HEAD is automatic: it runs the GET route and the response body is dropped. Switch it off with createRouter({ automaticHead: false }) if you need your own HEAD handling.
options: The GET route runs, and the server sends the headers without the body
The router answers 204 with an Allow header

questions.q: Why can a route middleware read context.request.getParam("id"), while a pipeline middleware cannot?
questions.explain: The order is: pipeline middleware, then matching, then route middleware, then the handler. Parameters only exist once a pattern has matched.
options: Pipeline middleware has no access to the request
Route middleware runs after the router has matched the route and copied its parameters onto the request; pipeline middleware runs before any route has matched
Parameters are only parsed when a route has middleware

questions.q: What does this print?

questions.q: A route /tasks/:id is registered inside router.group("/api/v1", …, { middleware: [a] }), inside a nested group "/tasks" with { middleware: [b] }, and has its own { middleware: [c] }. In what order do they run?
questions.explain: Group middleware lists add up from the outside in: the outer group's, then the inner group's, then the route's own.

questions.q: What is the main safety benefit of putting an API-key check on a group instead of on each route?
questions.explain: Repeating the same middleware on every route means one omission is an open door. A group applies it to every route registered inside it.
options: A new route added to the group cannot forget the check
Groups hide their routes from 404 responses
Group middleware runs before the CORS middleware

questions.q: Why does the generated example resource live under /api/v1/examples?

So CORS applies only to versioned routes

questions.q: A permission check reads the last role query value and your handler reads the first. A client sends ?role=viewer&role=admin. What is this attack called, and what is the safest fix?
questions.explain: Two layers picking different values from the same request is the bug. Refusing repeats with 400 for single-value parameters means every layer sees the same, single value.
options: Prototype pollution; use a null-prototype object
HTTP parameter pollution; refuse a repeated key for any parameter that must have one value

questions.explain: + is decoded as a space, and the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype are dropped, so a query can never pollute object prototypes.

questions.q: A client sends ?tag=home,urgent. What is ctx.query.tag?
questions.explain: Only a repeated key makes an array. A comma is an ordinary character; if you want comma lists, split them yourself and document it.

questions.q: With a default createRouter() and one route GET /tasks/:id, how many of these four requests find the route?
questions.explain: By default the router ignores the case of literal segments and a trailing slash, and it always collapses repeated slashes. All four spellings reach the same route.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The two options make case and the trailing slash significant. Repeated slashes are still collapsed: //tasks//7 is the same path in every mode.

questions.q: What is the strongest reason to choose caseSensitive: true and strictTrailingSlash: true?
questions.explain: A forgiving router answers many spellings of one resource. Other layers that match on the raw text do not know that, so strict routing keeps everyone looking at the same URL.
options: They are required for route parameters
Every resource then has exactly one URL, so caches and rules written in other layers (a CDN, a proxy) agree with the server

questions.q: Why does the Node adapter refuse GET /tasks/../admin with 400 instead of resolving it to /admin?

A proxy that blocks /admin* on the raw text would let it through while a resolving server served /admin; refusing it means every layer agrees
Because the router cannot match paths with dots
To save the cost of resolving the path

To keep the message under the length limit

questions.q: Write specificity(pattern): return one character per segment, "3" for a literal, "2" for a parameter (starts with :), "1" for a wildcard (starts with *). Then sort the patterns so the most specific comes first, comparing the strings from the left, and keep registration order for ties.
questions.explain: Comparing segment by segment from the left puts literals before parameters before wildcards. sort is stable, so equal routes keep their registration order, which is exactly the tie rule of the router.

questions.q: Write matchPattern(pattern, path) for patterns made of literals and :name parameters only. Return the parameters as an object, or undefined when the path does not match. Literals compare case-insensitively, parameter values are decoded with decodeURIComponent, and a decoded value containing / must fail the match.
questions.explain: Splitting on / before decoding is what keeps an encoded slash from creating a new segment; checking the decoded value refuses it as a parameter. Real routers add optional parameters, constraints and wildcards on top of this core.

questions.q: Write asArray(value) that turns a query value of type string | string[] | undefined into a string[] (like queryArray), and single(query, name) that returns the one value or undefined, and throws Error('Send "name" at most once') for a repeated key.

[ 'home', 'urgent' ] [ 'open' ] []
open undefined
Send "sort" at most once

questions.q: Write hasDotSegment(target): take the part before ?, split it on / and on \, decode each segment with decodeURIComponent (a segment that fails to decode counts as bad), and return true if any decoded segment is . or ...
questions.explain: Decoding before comparing catches the encoded forms, and splitting on backslashes catches the Windows spelling. Dots inside a segment (v1.2) and dots in the query are harmless.

questions.q: Write buildPath(pattern, params): replace every :name segment with encodeURIComponent(String(value)), and throw Error('Missing route parameter "name".') when a value is missing.
questions.explain: Encoding each value keeps it inside its own segment, so user data cannot change the shape of the path. This is what buildRoutePath from @zudojs/http does for you.

questions.q: Given a list of registered patterns (already sorted most specific first) and a match(path) function that returns the first pattern whose regular expression matches, write deadRoutes(samples): for each [pattern, samplePath] pair, report the pattern when the sample is answered by a different pattern.
questions.explain: This is the idea behind the route-table test: give every route one sample request and check that the route itself answers it. A shadowed route fails immediately, instead of in production.
